justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a relatively stable near-term outlook with modest upward drift over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 372 is anchored heavily on recent observed values and short-term momentum, assuming no major shock materializes overnight. The slight increase to 375 at one week reflects a small positive drift assumption, perhaps consistent with underlying trend or mean-reversion dynamics. By one month, the estimate of 382 incorporates a continued but gradual upward trajectory, though the pace remains modest because longer horizons force more regression toward any structural baseline rather than extrapolating short-term momentum indefinitely.

The confidence interval widths widen considerably as the horizon extends, which reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 65 units, driven primarily by normal day-to-day volatility. By one week, that range expands to about 117 units, incorporating uncertainty about whether any emerging trends will persist or reverse. At one month, the interval spans nearly 184 units, reflecting not just volatility accumulation but also genuine uncertainty about whether the underlying process will remain stationary or experience a regime shift. The asymmetry in the intervals is modest but intentional, reflecting slightly fatter downside tails due to the possibility of abrupt negative shocks compared to more gradual upside moves.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected macroeconomic deterioration, a sudden liquidity event, or a structural break in the data-generating process could push values well below the lower bounds, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst — such as a significant policy shift, a surprise demand surge, or a coordinated external intervention — could push values above the upper bounds. These tail risks are precisely what the 10% probability mass outside the intervals is meant to capture, but by construction they are treated as low-probability events under current information.

It is worth noting that all three intervals share the limitation of being conditioned on the information available at the time of the forecast. If the underlying process is non-stationary or subject to fat-tailed shocks — which many real-world series are — then even the one-month interval may be systematically too narrow. Forecasters routinely underestimate uncertainty at longer horizons, so these intervals should be treated as reasonable guides rather than precise probabilistic commitments, and they warrant updating as new data arrives.
